The physics of why your train window fogs up

Published 2026-10-06 17:30 UTC

Anyone who has ridden a train on a cold, rainy day knows the windows fog up. The explanation seems simple: warm, humid air from passengers' breath meets cold glass, and water condenses. But physicists who study the problem say the details involve a surprisingly deep fluid dynamics puzzle.

Condensation depends on a thin layer of air right next to the glass, called the boundary layer. In this layer, air moves slowly and its temperature changes rapidly from the warm cabin to the cold surface. Whether droplets form depends on how quickly heat and water vapor diffuse through this layer, which in turn depends on how air circulates in the carriage.

Researchers built a model of a train carriage and measured airflow with tiny tracer particles. They found that ventilation vents create swirling currents that sweep along some windows while leaving others in stagnant zones. Windows in stagnant zones fogged much faster, even when the overall cabin temperature and humidity were the same.

The shape of the droplets matters too. Fog consists of millions of tiny droplets that scatter light. When the glass is coated with a material that makes water spread into a thin film instead, the window stays clear even though water is still condensing on it. Many anti-fog coatings work this way.

Motion adds another layer of complexity. As a train speeds up, the outside of the glass cools faster because of wind, which increases condensation inside. Vibrations can cause small droplets to merge and run down the glass, creating streaks.

The researchers say understanding these effects could help engineers design better ventilation for vehicles, buildings and greenhouses, where condensation causes problems from mold to reduced light for plants.

The same physics explains why a car windshield clears faster when the defroster blows air directly onto the glass: fast-moving air thins the boundary layer and carries moisture away before droplets can form.
